messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: stepsizes
parts:
This is pretty much a question for Mike:

I was just wondering if it would make sense to adapt to multiple step sizes. The simplest approach would be to do a separate adaptation for each chain, then suppose they came up with step sizes a,b,c,d. Then in the HMC, we could rotate thru these 4 values for each chain. The advantage would be that if different step sizes are better for different parts of the space, we'd get multiple chances to get a good value. And a really crappy value would not kill a chain, as it would only be used 1/4 of the time (for simplicity I'm assuming 4 chains here).

We could use the same idea for adapting mass matrices. We'd have multiple mass matrices (or multiple scaling vectors, if we're just adapting on the diagonals).

Yes, I realize that RMHMC is much more sophisticated, but in the context of static Nuts, what do you think?

A

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] stepsizes
parts:
We currently have an option for jittering step size.

Communication across chains will require:

* inter-process communication and synchronization to run
in parallel

* running just warmup in sequence, saving results, then
restarting in sequence

Many of the things we'd have to do to the code to support
these two approaches would be shared. But then it brings
up how fine-grained we want inter-chain communication to be.
This is just one synch point, which is relatively easy compared
to more frequent and asynchronous inter-chain communication.

Another thought is that if we have the intention of covering
a space that might have varying geometry, we may want to design
the parallel warmup to try to do some kind of reasonable cover.
Right now, we're only trying to learn a single global mass matrix,
which as we know is inappropriate for hierarchical models like
the funnel.

- Bob

1. My first thought was to use info from different chains. But it would also be possible to have multiple step sizes (more generally, multiple mass matrices) within chains.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] stepsizes
parts:
So this kind of strategy would really be appropriate for posteriors with multiple modes, each with different curvature.
The big issues we're seeing are with models where the curvature changes continuously, and consequently almost
all of the chains will really average over the curvature instead of adapt to just a local region. In other words, trying
to get multiple chains with different step sizes will be difficult.

Then there's the issue of varying the step size. Without being able to select the step size based on the local curvature
you'll get significant inefficiencies.

I think the big potential gain with interchain communication is in learning the global curvature quickly (i.e. not limited
by large autocorrelation early in a single chain) which would speed up warmup.

Mike:

You're thinking big, which is fine, but I still see some potential gain from thinking small. In our experience, many times we've had a Stan model that's fit pretty well, but the occasional chain gets stuck in adaptation and ends up being a disaster. So I was thinking that this rotate-among-mass-matrices approach might help. I'm not thinking about multiple modes, I'm just thinking about how to avoid some of our current bottlenecks.

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] stepsizes
parts:
Yes, it's a failure of adaptation, but if we run 4 chains and each gives a different mass matrix, and 3 are good and 1 is bad, then rotating through the 4 will give us an efficiency of 3/4, which is far better than having 3 chains humming fine and 1 chain stuck in disaster mode.

We could even move form a 2-stage to a 4-stage process. Right now, stage 1 is adaptation and stage 2 is running the chains. One problem with the current system is that stage 1 can go very slowly, another problem is that if we get a shitty mass matrix in stage 1, we're fucked in stage 2. My above suggestion should fix the problem in stage 2, but we'd still be going slow in stage 1.

The new plan could be: stage -1 is initial adaptation giving initial mass matrices. Stage 0 is running by rotating thru the 4 mass matrices obtained in stage -1. Then Stage 1 is adaptation again. And Stage 2 is the production runs, with each chain rotating thru the 4 mass matrices obtained in stage 1. The point of Stages -1 and 0 in this new version is to more effectively move us away from bad places so we're less likely to get stuck in stage 1.

Yes, I know it's a bit of a hack, but perhaps there is a general principle here. If we have multiple chains and they are converging to different adaptations, we might as well take advantage of this information.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] stepsizes
parts:
I understand your motivation but I think tuning the more flexible adaptation will be able to remove
many of these cases instead of relying on some sampling procedure. HMC should be providing
us with enough information to get out of the tails provided we don't let the adaptation get in our way.

Also, I very much agree with your sentiment about using information from multiple chains. But once
we've built up an interchain/ensemble framework that would allow us to leverage that information
we would be able to build a more robust adaptation anyways.

I guess it depends how this new adaptation works. I'm frustrated with myself because I think if I'd thought of this rotating-mass-matrix thing a year ago, it could really have helped us, but maybe now we are close to a technology that will make the idea unnecessary.

In any case, though, even with a flexible adaptation, I'd think that in a non-Riemannian setting, a typical distribution would work better with an ensemble of mass matrices rather than a single mass matrix. And, with an ensemble, rotating through seems like a pretty robust way to get the benefits.

>>
>> We could even move form a 2-stage to a 4-stage process. Right now, stage 1 is adaptation and stage 2 is running the chains. One problem with the current system is that stage 1 can go very slowly, another problem is that if we get a shitty mass matrix in stage 1, we're fucked in stage 2. My above suggestion should fix the problem in stage 2, but we'd still be going slow in stage 1.
>>
>> The new plan could be: stage -1 is initial adaptation giving initial mass matrices. Stage 0 is running by rotating thru the 4 mass matrices obtained in stage -1. Then Stage 1 is adaptation again. And Stage 2 is the production runs, with each chain rotating thru the 4 mass matrices obtained in stage 1. The point of Stages -1 and 0 in this new version is to more effectively move us away from bad places so we're less likely to get stuck in stage 1.
>>

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] stepsizes
parts: > In any case, though, even with a flexible adaptation, I'd think that in a non-Riemannian setting, a typical distribution would work better with an ensemble of mass matrices rather than a single mass matrix. And, with an ensemble, rotating through seems like a pretty robust way to get the benefits.

I am not as confident in the ultimate utility as you are. The problem is how well can you actually learn the optimal distribution and what is the variance of that distribution? Even if you can learn it correctly you'll introduce a cost proportionally to the standard deviation in the best case -- in the case of hierarchical models where the distribution would be skewed the cost would be even worse.

Again, the only circumstance I can think of where such a strategy would work is when the optimal distribution is multimodal and in that case we have bigger issues to deal with.

The real issue here isn't that the target distribution has multiple scales and the adaptation of each chain is learning a unique scale but rather that the adaptation in one of the chains screws up and converges to a poor value that doesn't represent any of the correct scales.

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] stepsizes
parts: Yes, if one chain screws up, my thought it is that it is better to have 4 chains that are, effectively, running at 3/4 speed (because every fourth iteration is wasted by having a bad mass matrix) rather than having 3 chains going at full speed and 1 chain getting stuck.

messages.author: 29f6a893ff2525e2
messages.subject: Re: stepsizes
parts:
How do you detect disaster in a chain?

During burn-in, I allow a 'reset', which re-estimates a starting step size. I reapply find_reasonable_epsilon, and re-estimate a mass matrix.

I do this when alpha/nalpha < 1.0e-10 and depth >= maxDepth

This was purely from experience when the step size collapsed, and it seemed to do it when those conditions were observed.

Resets are common in optimisation algorithms, when certain conditions are observed.

Because my function/derivative evaluation is complex and I can multi thread at that level, I do not multi thread at the chain level. So I can easily communicate between chains. This is needed anyway when I use e.g. DREAM samplers. Rolling DREAM and other samplers into the mix of course also avoids any one chain becoming stuck. If you multi thread at the chain level (which I can understand is your preferred approach), then communicating becomes difficult, especially if the elapsed time per sample varies a lot - which it will do if each chain uses NUTS, and even more so if different chains use different samplers.

My current approach is to have a common stepsize etc. across all chains, so every chain is used as input into a common adaptor. This will also help avoid sticking.

Maybe there is some conflict between the best multi threaded implementation architecture, and the best single threaded algorithm? Which is the cart, which is the horse? If communication is rare, then having a chain waiting until all other chains have reached a 'checkpoint' should not be difficult to implement.

Trying to handle multiple modes which have different optimal step sizes/masss matrices is a whole other issue - and you certainly don't want a chain stuck in a single mode. I mix in DREAM mainly for this reason. Same for models with discrete variables.

I do, of course, jitter the step size. I jitter with a 10% Gaussian distribution, but I did try at one time with a gamma distribution.

It makes me wonder - does your implementation architecture easily allow a chain to rotate (or randomly choose) different samplers? Not just during burn-in? This may be long term a more important issue than the chain sticking problem.
